description: 20-turn transcript in the shape the app stores (CookieManager.ts / chat/route.ts). Used to probe the ~4 KB single-cookie ceiling (KI-004) — this fixture is ~2 KB as JSON before URL-encoding, so it should still fit; the generator below extends it past the limit.

value.content: HiPi, which one of you would pick TypeScript for a weekend hack?
Hitesh: TypeScript. Types are documentation that the compiler enforces, and for a weekend hack the setup cost is twenty minutes.
Piyush, do you agree?
Piyush: Mostly. For a throwaway script I would still reach for plain JS, but the moment a second person reads it, types pay for themselves.
What about testing a side project?
Hitesh: One smoke test on the critical path is worth more than a full pyramid on a side project nobody depends on.
How would you structure a Next.js app for a small team?
Piyush: App Router with thin route handlers, business logic in src/lib, and a rule that components never fetch directly from the database layer.
Should I add a database on day one?
Hitesh: No. Start with the smallest store that can lose data safely; migrate when the pain is measurable.
When do you reach for streaming responses?
Piyush: When the first token matters more than the last one — chat, logs, long generations. Otherwise keep the simple non-streamed path.
Any advice on prompt design?
Hitesh: Put the constraints where they cannot be missed, keep the persona separate from the task, and always test the empty and hostile inputs.
And on deployment?
Piyush: Pick the boring platform, pin your runtime, and make the health check the first thing you build.
Last one: how do you keep a demo honest?
Hitesh: Say what is not done. A demo that lists its own gaps is more trustworthy than one that pretends to be finished.
That's a good note to end on.
Piyush: Agreed. Ship the small thing, then make it obvious how to verify it.
